6.5 — Platforming Studio: The Gauntlet

Build day. Every skill from this unit — the flick, the honest ground check, the mercies, the counter — goes into one room that a stranger must finish without a single word from you. The grade is not difficulty and it is not art. The grade is clarity: a player who has never seen your cave should know where to go next by looking at it.

Studio Brief ~15 min

Everything in this room is yours to place. Read that again, because it is the thing people get wrong on build day: the cave scene ships with a floor and nothing else. There are no Coins in it, no Spikes in it, no Turrets in it. If your gauntlet needs a hazard, you drag it in from Assets/Prefabs and make it work — which means giving the Spikes a collider, the way you did in 2.2, and giving anything you want to pick up a collider and a tag the way you did in 2.1 and 6.4.

SectionWhat it testsWhat you must place yourself
1 — The gap A jump across a hole with a running start. Two platforms with a gap between them. Extend the floor by painting on the Collision tilemap, or drop in sprites with colliders — either is fine.
2 — The climb A jump up onto a ledge, then another. Raised surfaces. Measure the height against what your 6.1 numbers can actually reach — not against what looks right.
3 — The spike run Precision under threat. Spikes from Assets/Prefabs/Spikes, each with a solid collider you add, plus small platforms to cross them.
4 — The soft gate A promise: something visible you cannot have yet. A Coin from Assets/Prefabs, placed out of reach of one jump and reachable with two.
5 — The gauntlet's end A threat you pass rather than fight, and a clear finish. A ranged threat and a finish trigger. Use the turret from 3.1 if yours is working; an enemy or a second spike run is a legitimate substitute.
Architectural specification: the finish line.
  • The finish is a trigger, so which object needs the collider with Is Trigger ticked — the flag, or the player? What does 2.1 say about the minimum for an overlap to be reported at all?
  • Which callback fires, and what parameter type does it hand you? Which tag check tells you the thing that arrived was the player and not a stray projectile?
  • What does it print? Your HUD lives in Start and reads your stats — it is not in this scene, and it does not know a finish line exists. So the Console is still how a tester learns they finished.
  • Does the finish fire once, or every frame the player stands in it? How do you make it fire exactly once?
  • Should the finish do anything else — stop the player, print a time, count attempts? Decide, and be able to say why you stopped where you did.
Architectural specification: dying has to mean something.
  • What does your death rule from 2.2 actually do — reload a scene, or reset and move the player? Read your own code and state it in one sentence.
  • If you reload, the player reappears at wherever the Player instance sits in the saved scene. Is that the start of your gauntlet? If you dragged the Player to the start during Play mode, was that position saved when you stopped?
  • Where is your start pad — an actual object the player stands on, or just a remembered position? What happens to a tester's first thirty seconds if the room starts them mid-section?
  • If your death rule loads a scene by name or index, read Build Settings before you answer: which scene is index 0, and does it contain a Player? Find out rather than assuming.
  • What survives a death in your build — the coin count, the boots, the health — and what is lost? State it, then test it, then decide whether you accept the rule.
Architectural specification: the camera. Main Camera carries a follow script from Assets/Scripts/Package Scripts with two Inspector fields: an offset and a checkbox. One of those fields decides whether the camera follows the player vertically. Section 2 is a climb. Decide what the camera should do during that climb, change the setting if you need to, and be ready to justify it — a room you cannot see is not a room you designed.

Rules of the studio:

  • You may not explain the room verbally. Ever. The room teaches by layout or it does not teach.
  • Every section must be passable two ways, or with two different timing windows. A pixel-perfect single solution is a bug, not a challenge.
  • Keep a notes file open the whole time. Every "hmm" from a tester is a bug you have not built yet.
  • Build order that works: floor and walls first, then the start pad, then one section at a time — test each one alone before you chain them — and tune the 6.3 feel numbers last. Teams that tune feel first spend the afternoon tuning air.
Read Function-Level Examples ~10 min

Level design has a literature, and none of it is about video games. Read these for the principle, then name the section of your gauntlet each one is complaining about.

Example 1 — A theme park queue (comment only):

// The rope maze does not stop anyone. It just makes the wrong path
// obviously longer than the right one.

Example 2 — A furniture showroom (comment only):

// Every room is visible from the doorway. Nobody is ever told where to go.
// They are simply able to see it.

Example 3 — A bowling lane (comment only):

// The gutter is visible from the foul line, not discovered at the pins.
// A hazard you only meet at full speed is a hazard you cannot learn.

Example 4 — A building's fire escape (comment only):

// Two ways down from every landing, because on the day it matters
// one of them will be blocked.

Example 5 — An attempt counter at a climbing wall:

if (testerFell) attempts++; // the number that turns "hard" into "learning"

Socratic: Reading a Room

  1. The rope maze makes the wrong way slower without blocking it. Which section of your gauntlet does that, and which one just blocks?
  2. The showroom assumes the visitor can see the whole space. Can a tester see your section 4 gate from the moment they could possibly need it — or only after they have already walked past?
  3. The bowling alley puts the gutter where you can see it from the start. Where is your spike run visible from, and what speed is a tester moving when they first see it?
Playtest: Silent, With Numbers ~20 min

The silent-watching rules from 2.4 still apply — no hints, no pointing, no explaining. Today you also record numbers per section. Vague feedback is what you get when you did not write anything down.

SectionDeathsTime (seconds)What the tester said
1 — the gap
2 — the climb
3 — the spike run
4 — the soft gate
5 — the end

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Ship a five-section gauntlet that a stranger finishes without instructions
  • Say which unit skill each section tests, and point at the geometry that tests it
  • Place and build every hazard yourself — spikes with colliders, coins with tags, platforms with surfaces
  • State what your death rule does, where it puts the player, and what survives it
  • Collect death and time data instead of vibes, and make one numbered change per round
  • Commit and push
